title: Believe
subtitle: A five-session study on what Christians actually believe, and why it is both reasonable and life-giving.
summary:
This study is for new believers taking their first honest steps, for seekers who are circling the faith with real questions, and for small groups willing to slow down and ask what the gospel even is before anyone is asked to sign on to it. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book Believe, on whether there is a God at all and what kind, on who Jesus claimed to be and why the claim cannot be sidestepped, on whether he actually rose from a tomb, on faith and doubt and the difference between certainty and trust, and on what it costs and what it gives to follow him. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than in winning an argument.

This is not a study that treats doubt as the enemy or seekers as projects to be closed. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. Faith is not the absence of questions, and a faith that has never been tested is not strong, it is merely untested. Some objections to Christianity are bad and collapse under their own weight. Some are serious, honest, and have been asked by the church's best minds for two thousand years, and those deserve a real answer and not a slogan. The study holds both without flinching. Most of all it implicates the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He came to faith out of atheism, which means he has sat on the other side of the table and meant his objections. He was raised without a father, which shapes how he hears the word Father applied to God. He still has mornings the doubt comes back. He writes from inside the questions, not from a safe distance above them. So will you.
audience: New believers, seekers, small groups, and adult Sunday school

sessions.title: Is There Anyone There
sessions.aim: To ask the first question honestly, whether there is a God at all and what kind, and to refuse both the believer who treats the question as settled before it is asked and the skeptic who treats unbelief as the obvious default that needs no defending.
sessions.summary: A man told Bell after a talk that he wanted to believe but could not make himself, that the whole thing felt like wishing on a star, and he wanted to know how an honest person starts. He starts where everyone actually starts, with the question itself. Is there anyone there. Bell takes the strong form of two answers that want to silence each other. The first says belief is obvious, that the world so plainly declares a maker that only a fool says there is no God, and it is right that something rather than nothing is a fact that begs for an explanation, right that the order and beauty of things are not nothing. The second says unbelief is the grown-up default, that science has explained the gaps God used to fill and faith is a comfort for people who cannot bear a meaningless world, and it is right that some belief is exactly that, a crutch, a wish dressed as a fact. Bell will not let either win cheaply. The world does not prove God the way a theorem proves a conclusion, which checks the overconfident believer, and unbelief is not the neutral, cost-free default it pretends to be, because the atheist also has to explain why there is something instead of nothing, why the universe is the kind of place where minds can ask the question at all. The honest position is not that the case is closed but that the case is real, that the evidence points and does not coerce, and that a person can follow the pointing without pretending to a certainty no one has.

keyScripture.why: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky proclaims the work of his hands. The psalmist does not argue God into existence with a proof. He points, the way Jesus would later point at birds, treating the world itself as a witness that speaks without words to anyone willing to look.

discussion.q: Before tonight, what did you privately believe about God, that he is obviously there, that he is obviously not, or that you have simply never let yourself decide?
discussion.behind: Surface the default before defining anything. Most people in the room carry an unexamined verdict, often inherited rather than chosen, and they have rarely said it out loud. The point is not to settle the question yet but to expose the assumption and how little it has been examined. Land it on honesty, not consensus. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Bell says the world does not prove God the way a theorem proves a conclusion, but that it points. What is the difference between something that proves and something that points, and why does it matter here?
discussion.behind: Move the room off the demand for a knock-down proof. Many seekers think faith requires certainty and reject it for lack of one. The aim is to introduce the idea that evidence can genuinely point without coercing, the way a verdict rests on a weight of evidence and not a mathematical demonstration. Help them feel that this is how most real convictions are held.

discussion.q: Bell argues that unbelief is not the neutral, cost-free default it pretends to be, that the atheist also has to explain why there is something rather than nothing. Does that land, or do you want to resist it?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge of the session. Do not let it become a debate to be won. Keep it on the recognition that both belief and unbelief are positions with a burden, that no one stands on neutral ground. The honesty here levels the table and lets the seeker stop feeling like the only one being asked to defend a claim.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong form of the view that faith is a crutch, a comfort for people who cannot bear a meaningless world. What is true in that, and what does it leave out?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness. Some belief really is wishful, a fear of death dressed as conviction, and the seeker should hear the church admit it. The miss is that the charge cuts both ways, that unbelief can also be a wish, the wish to have no one to answer to. Make sure the room does not leave thinking only believers have motives.

discussion.q: Bell came to faith out of atheism, which means he once meant the objections he now answers. Where have you held a position mostly because it was the one you were handed, and never really chosen?
discussion.behind: Move from argument to self-implication. You are not hunting for converts tonight. You want each person, including you the leader, to admit how much of what they believe was inherited rather than examined, because honest faith and honest doubt both begin by owning what you actually think. Go first.

objections.objection: Science has explained everything religion used to explain. We do not need God to account for lightning or disease or the origin of species anymore, so God is just the shrinking gap in our knowledge, and one day the gap will close entirely.
objections.response: Sit with the half that is true, because Bell grants it. Science has indeed explained mechanisms that earlier generations attributed directly to God, and a faith that depends on God hiding in the gaps of our ignorance will keep losing ground as the gaps close. That kind of god is worth abandoning. Then make the distinction with care. Science explains how the universe works, the mechanism, the chain of cause and effect inside it. It does not and cannot explain why there is a universe at all for the mechanisms to run in, or why it is ordered in a way that minds can understand, or why anything exists rather than nothing. Those are not gaps in the science. They are questions the science assumes an answer to before it can begin. The God Christians mean is not a competing mechanism inside the universe. He is the reason there is a universe with mechanisms. To say science replaced him is to confuse the engine with the question of why there is a road.

objections.objection: If you only believe because you were born into a Christian family in a Christian country, your faith is just an accident of geography. Born in another place you would believe something else, so none of it is really true, it is just culture.
objections.response: Grant what is right, because much of it is. A great deal of belief is inherited, geographic, cultural, held without examination, and a faith that has never been anything but the local default deserves the suspicion. The church should say so. Then press the other edge gently. The argument proves too much, because it applies to everything you believe, including your unbelief. Born in a different time and place you would hold different politics, different morals, a different view of God, and that is equally true of the skeptic raised among skeptics. The accident of where you started tells you nothing about whether a thing is true, only about where you began looking. The question is not where your belief came from. The question is whether, having examined it as an adult, it turns out to be true. Bell did exactly that, from the other side, and changed his mind.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If God is real and is not the distant clockmaker but a Father who wants to be known, what in you most resists wanting that to be true?
sessions.practice: This week, do what the psalmist did. Once a day, go outside and look at something you did not make and cannot fully explain, the sky, a tree, your own hand, and stay with it long enough to feel the strangeness that it exists at all. Then ask the honest question, not is this proof, but what is this pointing to. Write down what came up, including the resistance, and do not judge it.
sessions.closingPrayer: God, if you are there, and we are asking honestly, you know that some of us have wanted you to be real and could not make ourselves believe, and some of us have wanted you not to be real and could not quite shake the sense that you are. Meet us in the wanting and the resisting both. We are tired of inherited answers we never chose. Give us the courage to look at the world and at ourselves without flinching, and if you are the one the heavens are declaring, let us begin to hear it. We come with our questions, not our conclusions. Amen.
reflection: What have I believed about God mostly because it was handed to me, and have I ever actually examined it as an adult who is free to decide?
Do I demand a proof of God that I do not demand for any other deep conviction I hold, and why might that be?
If unbelief is not the neutral default but a position with its own burden, what would I have to account for if there is no God, and have I ever tried?
sessions.teaching: Start where Bell starts, with a man after a talk. He said he wanted to believe but could not make himself, that the whole enterprise felt like wishing on a star, and he wanted to know how an honest person even begins. It is the right question, and it is the one this whole book is built to take seriously, because the worst thing the church can do to a seeker is rush him past the first question to get to the altar call. So we begin where everyone actually begins, not with how to have faith, which is where the eager want to begin, but with the harder and prior question. Is there anyone there at all. Take the two answers that want to silence each other, and take them at their strongest. The first says belief is obvious. It points to the sheer existence of things, the order of the cosmos, the fine-tuned constants, the beauty no survival pressure required, and it concludes that only a fool, in the psalmist's blunt phrase, says in his heart there is no God. And it is not entirely wrong. The fact that there is something rather than nothing is not a small thing to wave away. The universe did not have to exist, and it does, and it is the kind of place where the dust eventually wakes up and asks who made it, which is strange beyond telling. The second answer says unbelief is the grown-up default. It points to the long retreat of God before advancing science, to the way faith so often comforts exactly the people who most need comforting, and it concludes that belief is a crutch, a wish dressed up as a fact, a refusal to live in a universe that does not care. And this answer is not wrong either. Some belief is precisely that. There are people whose god is mostly a hedge against the fear of dying, and the honest believer has to admit it, because pretending otherwise hands the skeptic an easy and deserved victory. Now watch what happens when you refuse to let either answer take the whole field. The world does not prove God the way a theorem proves a conclusion. That destroys the overconfident believer's position, because the person who says it is just obvious has never sat across from a thoughtful atheist who is not being a fool, only being honest, and there are many. The evidence points. It does not coerce. A reasonable, intelligent, good-willed person can look at the same world and not be compelled, which means belief is a verdict reached on a weight of evidence, the way a jury reaches one, not a sum that forces itself on every mind. But here is the other edge, and it cuts just as deep. Unbelief is not the neutral, cost-free, obvious default it presents itself as. That destroys the skeptic's easy position, because the atheist does not get to stand on empty ground and make the believer do all the explaining. He, too, has to account for why there is something rather than nothing, why the universe is rationally ordered so that physics even works, why a meaningless accident of chemistry should produce minds that hunger for meaning and a sense of right and wrong that feels like more than preference. Saying I just lack a belief sounds modest, but the moment you ask the deep questions, the unbeliever has a worldview to defend like everyone else. There is no view from nowhere. Everyone is standing somewhere and has to account for the ground under their feet. And here I have to stand inside it, because I did not come to this from the cradle. I came to faith out of atheism. I have sat on the other side of this table and meant my objections, not as poses but as the honest convictions of a man who thought belief was for people who could not face the dark. I was also raised without a father, which means the word Father, when the Bible applies it to God, has never been an easy or sentimental word for me, and I will not pretend it is for everyone in this room. I write from inside the questions, not above them. So notice, finally, how Scripture itself handles the question, because it is not what we expect from a religion. The psalmist does not give a proof. He says the heavens declare the glory of God, the sky proclaims the work of his hands, day after day pours out speech and there are no words, no language, yet the voice goes out. He does not argue. He points. He treats the world as a witness that speaks to anyone willing to stand still and listen, the same way Jesus would later answer worry not with a syllogism but with look at the birds. The case for God is not a closed file. But it is a real case, and the honest seeker does not have to wait for a certainty no one possesses. He only has to be willing to follow the pointing and see where it leads, which is exactly what the next sessions ask.

scriptureStudy.note: The heavens declare the glory of God. The psalmist offers not a proof but a pointing, treating creation as a wordless witness. Belief begins with attention to what is already in front of us, not with a chain of logic.

His invisible attributes have been clearly perceived in the things that have been made. Paul claims the creation makes God knowable in a basic way to everyone, which is why he says no one is finally without excuse. The pointing is real, even if it does not coerce.

That they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us. Paul allows for groping, for feeling your way, treating honest seeking as a real path and not a failure of certainty.

Whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him. Faith here is not blind. It is the reasonable trust of one who has begun to seek and expects the seeking to be met.

The fool says in his heart there is no God. The verse is blunt, but notice it locates the denial in the heart, not only the head, suggesting that unbelief can be a posture of the will as much as a conclusion of the mind.
He has put eternity into the human heart. The Preacher names the ache that the world cannot fully satisfy, the hunger for meaning that an accidental universe would have no reason to produce.

The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. John claims a light already shines on every person, which means the seeker is not starting from nothing, only learning to name a light that was already there.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the long history of arguments for and against God, because the question is old and the church has done its best thinking under pressure, not in comfort. The classical theistic arguments, the cosmological argument that a contingent universe needs a necessary cause, refined by Thomas Aquinas in the thirteenth century, and the argument from design, have been pressed, answered, revised, and pressed again for centuries. A serious group should know that these were never meant to be knock-down proofs that compel assent. Aquinas himself called them ways, not demonstrations that force belief, paths along which the mind moves toward God. Set this beside the modern objections at their strongest. David Hume in the eighteenth century pressed hard on the design argument and on miracles, and the so-called new atheists of the early twenty-first century, Richard Dawkins and Christopher Hitchens among them, revived Hume's edge with great rhetorical force. Read them honestly. But weigh them against the serious replies, the work of philosophers like Alvin Plantinga on the rationality of belief in God, and writers like C. S. Lewis and later Timothy Keller, who argued that the deep human experiences of moral obligation, beauty, and longing are evidence that points beyond the material. The discipline this session requires is to refuse both the lazy believer who thinks the question is too easy and the lazy skeptic who thinks it is too settled. Hold instead that the existence of God is the kind of large question, like the meaning of a life or the reality of love, that the evidence genuinely bears on without ever closing like a math problem, and that a thoughtful person can follow the weight of it toward belief without pretending to a certainty that human beings do not get to have about anything that matters this much.
sessions.caseStudy: A graduate student named Daniel came to the group certain he was the only unbeliever in the room and braced for a fight. He had been told his whole childhood that real Christians did not have questions, and he had a list of them, the problem of suffering, the silence of God, the embarrassment of miracles in a scientific age. He expected to be argued at. Instead the leader asked him to state his strongest objection and then, to his surprise, agreed that it was a good one and that the church had often answered it badly. Daniel said later that the agreement disarmed him more than any argument could have, because he had come ready to defend against a sales pitch and found instead people who seemed as interested in the truth as he was. The work for the group here is to notice what actually moved him. It was not a clever proof. It was the discovery that his question was welcome, that no one needed him to lose so they could win. Ask your own room, where have you experienced the difference between being argued at and being taken seriously, and which one ever changed your mind about anything that mattered. The honest answer to that question is most of what this session is trying to teach.

sessions.title: Who Did Jesus Think He Was
sessions.aim: To take seriously the actual claims of Jesus rather than the polite modern version of him, and to refuse both the believer who skips past the scandal of those claims and the skeptic who reduces him to a nice teacher he plainly never was.
sessions.summary: Everyone has a Jesus. The skeptic has a wise moral teacher, the activist has a revolutionary, the comfortable have a gentle friend who agrees with them. The first question is whether any of these is the man in the documents, because the Jesus of the Gospels says things that explode the category of nice teacher. He forgives sins that were not committed against him, accepts worship, claims that before Abraham was, he is, and tells people that what they do with him decides what becomes of them. Bell takes the strong form of the modern instinct, that Jesus was a great moral teacher and we should keep the ethics and drop the supernatural claims. He grants the appeal. The teaching is luminous, and the world would be better for following the Sermon on the Mount. But the move does not work, and C. S. Lewis named why. A man who says the kinds of things Jesus said is not left to us as merely a great moral teacher. Either the claims are true, or the man making them was deluded on the scale of a person who calls himself a poached egg, or he was lying. Liar, lunatic, or Lord, but not, on the evidence, a sane and humble sage who merely taught us to love each other. Then the turn. The scandal is not that Christianity asks us to admire Jesus. Plenty of people admire him. The scandal is that he does not leave admiration as an option, that he asks the one thing a teacher never asks, which is everything, and stakes it on who he is and not only on what he said.

keyScripture.why: Jesus tells a paralyzed man his sins are forgiven, and the scribes rightly ask who can forgive sins but God alone. They understood the claim better than the modern admirers do. Jesus was not offering moral advice. He was assuming a prerogative that belongs to God, and he did it on purpose.

discussion.q: Before tonight, who was Jesus to you, a teacher, a myth, a friend, a figure you admired from a distance, and where did that picture come from?
discussion.behind: Open on the inherited Jesus before the documents get a vote. Almost everyone carries a version assembled from culture rather than from reading the Gospels. The aim is to expose the gap between the comfortable Jesus we have absorbed and the strange one in the text, so the rest of the session has somewhere to go.

discussion.q: The Jesus of the Gospels forgives sins, accepts worship, and claims to predate Abraham. If you only ever heard the gentle-teacher version, what is your honest reaction to those claims, and to having missed them?
discussion.behind: Get the room to feel the scandal that the sanitized version hides. Many have genuinely never noticed these claims because no one pointed them out. The aim is recognition, the small shock of realizing the actual figure is far stranger and more demanding than the cultural one.

discussion.q: Bell takes seriously the wish to keep Jesus the ethics and drop the supernatural claims. What is appealing about that move, and why does Lewis say it cannot honestly be made?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The wish is reasonable and the ethics are genuinely admirable. The miss is that the man teaching the ethics also made claims that, if false, would discredit his judgment entirely, so you cannot keep him sane and humble while throwing out half of what he said. Help the room feel the logic of the trilemma without using it as a club.

discussion.q: Lewis says we are not left the option of calling Jesus merely a great moral teacher, that it is liar, lunatic, or Lord. Where do you want to escape that, and is the escape honest?
discussion.behind: Let people push on the trilemma, because thoughtful skeptics have, raising the legend option, that the claims were put in his mouth later. Take it seriously rather than dismissing it, and note it pushes the question to the next session on the evidence. The aim is honesty about where each person actually stands, not forcing a verdict.

discussion.q: Bell says the scandal is not that Jesus asks to be admired but that he asks for everything. Where in your own life do you keep Jesus at the level of admiration precisely to avoid the level of surrender?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication. Admiration is safe and costs nothing, and most of us, the leader included, prefer it. The aim is honest recognition that we domesticate Jesus into a teacher exactly so we never have to deal with him as a Lord. Go first, and keep it gentle.

objections.objection: Jesus was a great moral teacher, maybe the greatest, and that is enough. Keep the love your enemies and the care for the poor and leave the supernatural claims behind. You do not have to think he was God to learn from him.
objections.response: Bell grants the appeal fully, because the teaching really is luminous and the world would be better for following it. But take the move seriously enough to see why it collapses. The same man who taught us to love our enemies also said that he and the Father are one, that he could forgive sins, that he would judge the living and the dead, and that what a person does with him settles their eternity. Now, if those claims are false, the man making them was not a wise and humble teacher. He was either lying, which ruins the moral authority you wanted to keep, or he was profoundly deluded about his own identity, which ruins his judgment about everything else. As Lewis put it, you can call him a liar or a lunatic, or you can fall at his feet and call him Lord, but the one thing you cannot do, not honestly, is the patronizing thing of calling him a great human teacher while ignoring the claims that, if untrue, would make him no such thing.

objections.objection: He never actually said any of that. The divine claims were added by the church decades later to build a religion. The real Jesus was a Jewish teacher, and the God talk is legend that grew up around him.
objections.response: This is the most serious version of the objection, and it deserves more than a wave, so treat it honestly and then point ahead. It is true that legends grow, and the question of what Jesus actually said is a real historical question, not an insult to the faith. But legend takes generations, and the earliest sources, including creeds Paul quotes that scholars date to within a few years of the crucifixion, already proclaim Jesus as risen Lord, far too early for myth to have replaced memory. The Gospels were written within living memory of eyewitnesses, some of whom would have contradicted invention. The honest path is not to assume the claims were added, nor to assume they were not, but to ask what the evidence actually supports, which is exactly the question of the next session, when we look at whether anything happened at that tomb. Hold the question open. Do not let anyone close it cheaply in either direction.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If Jesus is who he said he was, and not merely the teacher you can admire from a safe distance, what would change tomorrow morning, and is that the real reason you keep him at arm's length?
sessions.practice: This week, read the Gospel of Mark straight through, slowly, as if you had never heard of it, which takes about an hour. Do not study it. Just meet the man in it. Mark down every place he says or does something that a merely human teacher would have no business saying or doing. At the end, ask yourself honestly which of the three doors you are standing in front of, and which one you are avoiding.
sessions.closingPrayer: Jesus, we have made you small enough to admire and safe enough to ignore, a teacher we can quote and a friend who never asks for anything. Forgive us for the Jesus we invented to avoid the one who is real. Give us the courage to read the documents and meet you as you actually are, the one who forgives sins and accepts worship and asks for everything. We do not all believe yet, and we will not pretend we do. But we are willing to look. Show us who you think you are, and give us the honesty to deal with the answer. Amen.
reflection: Which Jesus have I been carrying, and how much of him came from the Gospels and how much from a culture that prefers him tame?
If the trilemma is fair, that he was liar, lunatic, or Lord, which door am I standing in front of, and which am I working hardest to avoid?
Where do I keep Jesus at the level of admiration precisely because admiration costs me nothing and surrender would cost me everything?
sessions.teaching: Everyone has a Jesus. The skeptic keeps a wise moral teacher, a first-century rabbi with unusually good ethics. The activist keeps a revolutionary who took the side of the poor against the powerful. The comfortable keep a gentle friend who, conveniently, agrees with all of their opinions. The trouble with all of these is the same trouble. None of them is the man in the documents, and the first honest task is to set our inherited Jesus down and pick up the one who actually speaks in the Gospels, because that one is far stranger and far more demanding than any of the versions we prefer. Read the texts without the soft focus and watch what he says. He tells a paralyzed man his sins are forgiven, and the religious experts in the room, who were not idiots, understand exactly what he has done and are scandalized, because everyone knew that only God can forgive sins committed against God. He accepts worship rather than refusing it the way every honest prophet and angel in the Bible refuses it. He says that before Abraham was, he is, deliberately taking the divine name onto his own lips, and his hearers pick up stones, because they understood the claim perfectly. He says he will judge the living and the dead, that what a person does with him decides their eternity, that he and the Father are one. These are not the marginal sayings of the tradition. They are everywhere, woven through the earliest material, and they are not the sort of thing a humble moral teacher says. So take the modern instinct at its strongest, because it is the one most people in the room are leaning on. It says keep the ethics and drop the metaphysics. Keep love your enemies and turn the other cheek and care for the least of these, which are magnificent, and quietly let go of the supernatural claims, which are embarrassing. You do not have to believe he was God to learn from him, the thinking goes, any more than you have to deify Socrates to learn from Socrates. Grant the appeal, because it is real. The teaching is luminous, and a world that actually lived the Sermon on the Mount would be a better world by any measure. But here is where the move breaks, and C. S. Lewis named the break more sharply than anyone before him. A man who was merely a man and said the kinds of things Jesus said would not be a great moral teacher. He would be on a level with a man who says he is a poached egg, or else he would be the devil of hell. The claims are too large to be the harmless eccentricity of a wise man. If a teacher tells you he can forgive your sins and will judge the world and existed before Abraham, and it is not true, then he is not wise and he is not humble. He is either deceiving you, which destroys his moral authority, or he is sincerely deluded about his own identity on a scale that destroys his credibility about everything else, including the ethics you wanted to keep. You are shut up to a hard choice. Liar, lunatic, or Lord. The one option the evidence does not leave open is the popular one, the patronizing pat on the head that calls him a fine human teacher while ignoring the very claims that, if false, would make him nothing of the kind. Now, the thoughtful skeptic has a fourth door, and we should name it honestly rather than pretend the trilemma is airtight. He may say there is a fourth L, legend, that Jesus never made these claims and the church put them in his mouth later. That is a serious objection, the most serious one, and it is not a sign of weak faith to feel its force. It pushes the whole question onto the ground of history, onto whether the sources are early and reliable, which is exactly where the next session goes. Hold it open. But notice what the legend theory concedes even as it objects, that the Jesus who comes down to us in the actual documents is not a mild teacher but a man making staggering claims, so that the only way to keep him mild is to assume, in advance, that the documents are wrong. And here I have to implicate myself, because I spent years preferring the admired Jesus to the real one. Admiration is safe. You can admire a man across a great distance and never have to move an inch of your life. What I did not want, what I think most of us do not want, is the thing he actually asks, which is the one thing no mere teacher has the right to ask. Socrates asks you to think. Aristotle asks you to reason. Jesus asks you for everything, your allegiance, your obedience, your very self, and he stakes the demand not on the brilliance of his arguments but on the claim of who he is. That is the scandal, and it cannot be smoothed away. The question this session leaves you with is not whether Jesus was admirable. Almost everyone grants that. The question is the one his own words force, the one I avoided for years. Who did he think he was, and what will you do with the answer.

scriptureStudy.note: Jesus forgives the paralytic's sins, and the scribes ask who can forgive sins but God alone. They grasped the claim exactly. Jesus was not moralizing. He was assuming a divine prerogative in plain view.
Before Abraham was, I am. Jesus takes onto his own lips the divine name God gave Moses, and his hearers immediately pick up stones, because they understood it as a claim to deity, not a metaphor.

I and the Father are one. The crowd again moves to stone him, and when he asks why, they answer that it is because he, a man, makes himself God. His opponents understood the claim more clearly than his modern admirers.

He taught them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes. Even his manner was a claim. The rabbis cited prior authorities. Jesus spoke as the authority, saying you have heard it said, but I say to you.

I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me. This is not the modesty of a teacher pointing past himself to the truth. He makes himself the way to God, the single door.

Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed. And Jesus said, I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power. Under oath, facing death, he affirms the claim, which liars under threat usually retract.

But who do you say that I am. Jesus refuses to let the question stay at the level of others' opinions and presses it onto the individual. It remains the question every reader of the Gospels is finally asked.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the question of the historical Jesus, because the claim that the divine Jesus is a later invention has a long scholarly history and a serious group should know its shape rather than fear it. The various quests for the historical Jesus, beginning in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries and running through the work of the Jesus Seminar in the late twentieth, attempted to strip away supposed legend and recover a merely human teacher underneath. Read these honestly, because the questions they raise about sources and dating are real questions, not attacks to be repelled. But weigh them against the serious historical replies. Scholars such as N. T. Wright, Richard Bauckham, who argued in Jesus and the Eyewitnesses that the Gospels rest on named eyewitness testimony, and the broad recognition that the creed Paul cites in First Corinthians fifteen, proclaiming the death, burial, and resurrection of Christ, can be dated to within a handful of years of the events, far too early for legend to have displaced memory. The discipline here is to refuse both the credulity that will not examine the sources and the skepticism that has already decided the supernatural is impossible and reads the evidence to fit. Note as well that the trilemma of Lewis was never meant as a complete proof but as a clearing of the ground, a way of removing the comfortable middle option so that the real question, did this happen, can be asked without the distraction of a tame Jesus who never existed in any source we have. The most honest position a seeker can hold at the end of this session is that the documents present a Jesus who claimed to be God, that this claim is early and not a late accretion, and that what remains to be examined is whether the central event the documents report, the resurrection, actually occurred.
sessions.caseStudy: A woman named Renata had spent twenty years as a comfortable churchgoer who loved the gentle-teacher Jesus, the one who blessed children and forgave the woman caught in adultery and said let the one without sin cast the first stone. When the group read the Gospel of Mark straight through, she came back the next week unsettled. I have been reading around the hard parts my whole life, she said. I knew the kind sayings by heart and I had somehow never noticed him forgiving sins or accepting worship or telling people he would judge the world. She had built a Jesus out of the verses that comforted her and quietly skipped the ones that made a claim. What troubled her was not that the claims were there but that she had spent two decades avoiding them to keep her faith easy. The work for the group is to sit with what Renata discovered, that a faith can be sincere and long-held and still rest on a Jesus we assembled to our own liking. Ask your room gently, which sayings of Jesus do you know by heart, and which ones have you been reading around, and what would change if you let the whole figure speak rather than only the parts that ask nothing of you.

memoryVerse.text: Jesus said to him, I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.

sessions.title: The Tomb
sessions.aim: To put the central claim of the faith where it belongs, on the table as a historical question, and to refuse both the believer who treats the resurrection as a mood and the skeptic who waves it away without ever weighing the actual evidence.
sessions.summary: Christianity is not a philosophy that happens to have a founder. It is a claim about an event, that a man who was publicly executed was, three days later, alive again, and that hundreds of people said they saw him. Paul himself stakes the entire thing on it, saying that if Christ has not been raised, the faith is worthless and Christians are to be pitied above all people. The first question is whether the event can be examined at all, or whether it is the kind of thing you simply believe or do not. Bell takes the strong form of the skeptic, that dead people do not rise, that miracles are by definition the least probable explanation, and that any natural account, theft, hallucination, the wrong tomb, a swoon, is more likely than a resurrection. He grants the force of it. Dead people do not rise, which is exactly what makes the claim worth examining rather than assuming. But the natural explanations each have to account for a stubborn set of facts, the empty tomb that the authorities could have refuted by producing a body, the appearances to many at once, the conversion of skeptics and enemies, and above all the willingness of the first witnesses to die for a claim they were in a position to know was false. Then the turn. The resurrection is not asked of us as a leap in the dark. It is offered as the best explanation of a set of facts that the alternatives strain to explain, the kind of inference a historian or a jury makes, not a feeling the believer works up.

keyScripture.why: If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain. Paul does not protect the faith from the question. He stakes everything on a falsifiable claim, telling the skeptic exactly where to aim, which is the opposite of a religion that hides from scrutiny.

discussion.q: Paul says if Christ has not been raised, the whole faith is worthless and Christians should be pitied. What does it tell you that the faith stakes everything on a single event that could, in principle, be disproven?
discussion.behind: Open on the falsifiability, because it surprises people. Most expect religion to insulate itself from disproof, and here is the apostle handing the skeptic the lever. The aim is to feel that this is not the move of a system built on wishful thinking but of one that claims something happened.

discussion.q: Bell grants the skeptic's strongest point, that dead people do not rise, so a miracle is by definition the least likely explanation. Why does he say that very fact is a reason to examine the claim rather than dismiss it?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The skeptic is right that resurrection is wildly improbable on its face, and the believer must grant it rather than pretend it is ordinary. The turn is that the improbability is why the early witnesses needed extraordinary reasons to believe it, and why their behavior demands an explanation. Help the room weigh, not just assume.

discussion.q: Walk through the natural explanations together, that the body was stolen, that the witnesses hallucinated, that they went to the wrong tomb, that Jesus only fainted. Which feels most plausible to you, and what does it have to explain?
discussion.behind: Get the room to actually do the work rather than receive a conclusion. Take each theory seriously and ask what it must account for, especially the public empty tomb and the group appearances. The aim is the experience of weighing alternatives like a juror, so faith is reasoned and not merely asserted.

discussion.q: The first witnesses suffered and died rather than recant. People die for things they believe are true, but these were people in a position to know whether it was true. Why does Bell think that matters so much?
discussion.behind: Land the strongest single point carefully. Note the distinction, that many die for sincere beliefs, but the apostles were not believing a report, they were claiming to be eyewitnesses, so for them the choice was die for what you know happened or expose a lie you invented. Help the room feel the weight of that without overclaiming it as airtight.

discussion.q: Bell admits the doubt still visits him on some mornings, that he has stood at the edge of the same question and felt the floor move. Where does the resurrection feel most real to you, and where does it feel hardest to believe?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication and honesty. The leader must model that doubt is not the enemy of faith but often its companion. Invite people to name both the pull and the resistance without resolving them. Go first. The point is honest weighing toward Christ, not a forced verdict tonight.

objections.objection: Dead people do not come back to life. A miracle is by definition the most improbable thing that could happen, so any natural explanation, even an unlikely one, is automatically more reasonable than a resurrection. The evidence would have to be impossible.
objections.response: Bell grants the premise rather than dodging it. Dead people do not rise, which is precisely why no first-century Jew was expecting an individual to be raised in the middle of history, and why the disciples did not believe it at first either but thought it nonsense. The improbability is real. But notice what the principle, prefer any natural explanation, actually costs when you apply it. You then have to commit to a specific natural explanation and defend it, and each one buckles under a particular fact. The stolen body has to explain why the authorities, who wanted the movement dead, never simply produced the corpse. The hallucination has to explain group appearances to many at once, including skeptics, since hallucinations are private. The swoon has to explain how a flogged and crucified man pushed a stone away and convinced people he was the conqueror of death. The honest skeptic does not get to rest in a vague it must have been something natural. He has to name the something and watch it strain against the facts, and Bell's claim is only that the resurrection explains them better.

objections.objection: People die for false beliefs all the time. Suicide bombers die for their faith. The martyrdom of the apostles proves they were sincere, not that they were right, so it proves nothing about whether the resurrection actually happened.
objections.response: This is a sharp objection and it deserves the precise answer, not a dodge. It is completely true that sincerity is not truth, and that people throughout history have died bravely for things that were false. But mark the distinction Bell insists on. The modern martyr dies for a belief he received from someone else, a conviction about events he did not witness. The apostles were not in that position. They were claiming to be the eyewitnesses, the ones who said we ate with him after, we touched him, we were there. So for them, and only for them, the choice was not die for something you sincerely believe. It was die for something you personally either saw or fabricated. Many people will die for a belief they think is true. Almost no one will be tortured to death to protect a lie they themselves made up, when a single recantation would end the pain. That does not prove the resurrection like a theorem. But it removes the easy theory that the disciples simply invented it, because invented lies do not usually survive the rack.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you became persuaded that the tomb was actually empty and the man was actually alive, what is the first thing in your life you suspect you would not want to change, and why does that matter more than the evidence to you?
sessions.practice: This week, do the work of a juror rather than a spectator. Take one of the natural explanations for the empty tomb, the one you personally find most plausible, and spend twenty minutes honestly trying to make it account for all the facts, the empty tomb, the appearances, the willingness to die. Write down where it holds and where it strains. Then sit, just for a moment, with the possibility that the simplest explanation is the one Christians have always given.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, if you were raised, then everything is different, and if you were not, then we are wasting an evening on a beautiful lie, and Paul says so himself. We do not want a faith built on pretending. We want to know what happened. For those of us who believe, steady us when the doubt comes back in the dark. For those of us who cannot yet believe, give us the patience to weigh it honestly rather than dismiss it out of habit. If the tomb was empty because you walked out of it, make us willing to deal with a living person and not just an old story. Amen.
reflection: Have I ever actually examined the evidence for the resurrection, or have I only assumed a conclusion, in either direction, and called the assumption a verdict?
Which natural explanation do I lean on, and have I honestly tested whether it accounts for the empty tomb, the appearances, and the willingness of the witnesses to die?
If I find the resistance is not really about the evidence but about what believing would cost me, what does that tell me about where my real objection lives?
sessions.teaching: Christianity is not, at its root, a philosophy of life that happens to have a charismatic founder attached. Strip away everything else and the irreducible core is a claim about an event in history. A man named Jesus was publicly arrested, tried, flogged, and executed by professional Roman executioners who did this for a living and did not make mistakes about whether a man was dead. He was buried. And three days later, his tomb was found empty, and over the following weeks more than five hundred people, in groups and alone, indoors and out, claimed to have seen him alive, eaten with him, touched him. That is the claim. Not that his teaching lived on, not that his spirit was somehow still with them, but that the dead man was bodily alive again. And the remarkable thing, the thing that should arrest the skeptic and the believer alike, is that the faith does not hide this claim behind a wall of mystery. Paul puts it on the table and hands the skeptic the knife. If Christ has not been raised, he writes, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain, and we are of all people most to be pitied. That is not the language of a man protecting a belief from scrutiny. That is a man staking everything on a single event and telling you exactly where to aim if you want to bring the whole thing down. So the first question is whether the event can even be examined, or whether resurrection is the kind of claim that simply lies outside evidence, something you either feel or do not. And here we have to take the skeptic's objection at full and fair strength, because it is the honest one and the believer who waves it away has not understood it. Dead people do not rise. That is not a prejudice, it is the most reliable observation in human experience, confirmed every single day. A miracle, by its very definition, is the least probable kind of event, and so, the skeptic reasons, any natural explanation, however unlikely, must be preferred to a supernatural one. If the choice is between a body being stolen and a corpse reanimating, the theft wins automatically, because theft happens and resurrection does not. Grant it. Grant all of it. Dead men do not rise, which is precisely why no one in the first century was expecting this, why the disciples themselves first heard the women's report as an idle tale and did not believe it, why Thomas demanded to put his hand in the wounds. The improbability is not a problem the believer should hide from. It is the very reason the event is worth examining instead of assuming, in either direction. But watch what happens when you stop saying it must have been something natural in the abstract and force yourself to name the something. The vague preference for a natural explanation has to become a specific theory, and every specific theory has to account for a stubborn cluster of facts that will not go away. Take the stolen body. Who stole it. If enemies took it to stop the movement, they had only to produce the corpse the moment the disciples started preaching resurrection in the same city weeks later, and the movement dies in an afternoon. They did not, which strongly suggests they could not. If the disciples took it, we are back to men dying for what they knew to be a fraud. Take the hallucination. Grief produces visions, true, but hallucinations are private, interior, one to a person, and the records describe groups seeing him at once, including a hardened skeptic like Paul and a brother like James who had not believed. Take the swoon, that Jesus merely fainted and revived in the cool tomb. This asks us to believe that a man scourged to the bone and pierced through, sealed in a rock tomb without food or medicine, not only survived but unwound his own grave clothes, moved a stone that took several men to move, overpowered or slipped past the guard, and then appeared to his followers in such a state that they worshiped him as the risen conqueror of death rather than rushing him to a physician. Each theory can be stated. None of them carries the weight without groaning. And then there is the single fact that has unsettled honest skeptics for two thousand years, the behavior of the witnesses. People die for false beliefs constantly, and so the bare fact of martyrdom proves only sincerity, not truth. The objection is correct as far as it goes, and we must say so. But the apostles were not in the position of the ordinary martyr who dies for a report he received and trusts. They were claiming to be the eyewitnesses themselves, the ones who said we saw him, we touched him, we ate with him after. For them, and for them uniquely, the choice under torture was not die for something you believe but die for something you either saw with your own eyes or made up with your own mouth. People will suffer for a conviction they hold to be true. Almost no one will be flogged and crucified and beheaded, one after another, refusing to recant, in order to protect a lie they personally invented, when a single word would stop the pain. That does not prove the resurrection the way two and two make four. History does not deal in that kind of proof, and neither does a courtroom. But it does something nearly as powerful. It makes the resurrection the best explanation of a body of evidence the alternatives can only strain to cover, the inference a fair juror draws, not a feeling a believer manufactures. And I will not stand over this as a man for whom it is all settled and easy, because it is not, even now. The doubt still visits me on certain gray mornings, when the floor seems to move and the whole thing feels like a story we told ourselves against the dark. I came to this from unbelief, and unbelief knows the way back to my door. So I am not asking you to feel a certainty I do not always feel. I am asking you to do what I had to do, to stop treating the resurrection as a mood to be summoned or dismissed and start treating it as a claim to be weighed, the most consequential claim ever made, offered not as a leap into the dark but as the best account of why that tomb was empty and those frightened men became people who would rather die than say it never happened.

scriptureStudy.note: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day, in accordance with the Scriptures. This is the earliest creed, material Paul received and passed on, dated by scholars to within a few years of the events, far too early for legend.

He appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive. Paul names living witnesses, in effect inviting the reader to go and ask them, which is not how someone writes who is inventing a story.

If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain. Paul stakes the whole faith on a falsifiable event and refuses to protect it from the test, which is the move of someone who believes it actually happened.

These words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them. The first reaction of the disciples themselves was disbelief, which undercuts the idea that they were credulous men primed to imagine a resurrection.

Thomas demands to put his hand in the wounds and will not believe on report alone. The Gospel preserves the doubter rather than hiding him, treating honest demand for evidence as a real and answerable thing.

The authorities pay the guards to say the disciples stole the body while they slept. Even the counter-story assumes an empty tomb, conceding the one fact every theory has to explain, that the body was gone.
This was not done in a corner. Paul tells a Roman official the events were public and checkable, appealing to facts the hearer could investigate, not to a private revelation no one could test.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the historical case for the resurrection in earnest, because this is the point where Christianity invites investigation rather than retreat, and a serious group should know the shape of the argument. Historians who study the question, believing and skeptical alike, tend to agree on a core set of facts often called the minimal facts, that Jesus died by crucifixion, that his tomb was found empty, that various individuals and groups had experiences they took to be appearances of the risen Jesus, and that the disciples were transformed from frightened deserters into bold proclaimers willing to die. The debate is not usually about these facts but about their best explanation. Read the strongest skeptical accounts, including the work of scholars like Bart Ehrman who grant the disciples' experiences while attributing them to grief, vision, and cognitive dissonance rather than to a literal rising. Weigh them honestly against the work of N. T. Wright, whose massive study The Resurrection of the Son of God argues that neither pagan nor Jewish categories of the time can account for the specific shape of the early Christian claim, and the long line of writers, including Frank Morison, whose Who Moved the Stone began as an attempt to disprove the resurrection and became the opposite, and Timothy Keller, who pressed the point that a movement built on bodily resurrection could not have survived a day in first-century Jerusalem if a body could be produced. The discipline is to refuse both the credulity that has never examined the alternatives and the closed skepticism that rules out the supernatural before looking, deciding in advance that no evidence could ever count. The honest seeker asks the historian's question, not which explanation do I prefer, but which explanation accounts for all the facts with the least strain, and then follows the answer even if it costs him the comfortable distance from which he started.
sessions.caseStudy: An attorney named Marcus volunteered, half joking, that he could pick apart the resurrection the way he picked apart weak testimony in court, so the leader asked him to actually try, in front of the group, taking the case for the prosecution. He chose the stolen-body theory and built it carefully, and then, being honest, he stopped himself. The problem, he said, is that I cannot explain why the prosecution, the authorities who wanted this dead, never produced the body. In a real trial that ends it. You produce the corpse and the whole case collapses, and they had every reason to and they did not. He sat back, visibly unsettled by his own argument. Then he said the thing that mattered most. I think I have spent years assuming a natural explanation without ever making myself name one and test it. The work for the group is to do what Marcus did, to stop preferring a natural explanation in the abstract and force it into the open where it can be examined. Ask your room, have you ever actually built the case against the resurrection, not waved at it, but built it, and tested whether it carries the weight, or have you held a verdict you never put on trial.

memoryVerse.text: Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, and he was buried, and he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures.

sessions.title: Faith and the Honest Doubt
sessions.aim: To recover what faith actually is, the reasonable trust of a person who has weighed the evidence, and to refuse both the believer who treats doubt as sin and the skeptic who treats faith as the willful belief of things you know are not true.
sessions.summary: The word faith has been ruined from both directions. The skeptic hears it as believing things without evidence, even against evidence, the deliberate switching off of the mind. Many believers hear doubt the same way, as the opposite of faith, a failure to be hidden and confessed. The first question is what the Bible actually means by the word, because it is neither of those. Bell takes the strong form of the skeptic's definition, that faith is belief without proof, a leap in the dark. He grants there is a kind of religion that is exactly that, blind, willful, anti-intellectual, and that it has done real harm. But the faith of the Bible is not belief without evidence. It is trust placed in a person on the basis of what you have come to know about them, the same kind of trust you place in a surgeon, a spouse, a pilot, never with total certainty, always with enough warrant to act. Then the turn on doubt. Doubt is not the enemy of faith. The opposite of faith is not doubt but unbelief, the settled refusal to trust, and doubt is something else entirely, the honest wrestling of a person who is still in the relationship, still asking. The father who cried I believe, help my unbelief, did not have his faith rejected. He had his son healed. The study refuses to shame the doubter, because a faith that has never been questioned is not strong, only untested, and Bell, who came to belief from the far side of unbelief, knows the difference from the inside.

keyScripture.why: The father cries out, I believe, help my unbelief. He holds faith and doubt in the same breath, and Jesus does not rebuke the mixture. He heals the boy. The verse stands as Scripture's own refusal to treat honest doubt as the disqualifier the church often makes it.

discussion.q: When you hear the word faith, what does it mean to you, believing without evidence, trusting a person, hoping against the odds, or something you have never quite defined?
discussion.behind: Surface the working definition, because almost everyone has absorbed the skeptic's version, faith as belief without proof, even many believers. The aim is to expose how unexamined the word is before offering the biblical sense, so the rest of the session has traction.

discussion.q: Bell says biblical faith is not belief without evidence but trust in a person based on what you have come to know of them, like trusting a surgeon or a spouse. Does that reframe faith for you, and where does it still feel like a stretch?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The reframe is genuine and important, faith as warranted trust rather than blind belief. But let people name where it still feels like more, where the trust outruns the evidence, because all trust does, and that is honest rather than something to paper over.

discussion.q: The opposite of faith, Bell argues, is not doubt but unbelief, the settled refusal to trust, while doubt is the wrestling of someone still in the relationship. How does that distinction land on your own experience of doubting?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. Many in the room carry secret doubts they believe disqualify them. The aim is the relief of distinguishing doubt, which is honest engagement, from unbelief, which is a closed door. Help the doubter hear that their wrestling is a form of holding on, not letting go.

discussion.q: The father in Mark says I believe, help my unbelief, and Jesus heals the boy anyway. What does it do to you that Jesus answered a mixed and imperfect faith rather than demanding a pure one first?
discussion.behind: Land the mercy of the text. Many believe they must resolve all doubt before they can come or be heard. The aim is to feel that Jesus meets the divided heart, that the qualification for coming is not certainty but the willingness to bring even a faith you are not sure of. Keep it tender.

discussion.q: Bell says a faith that has never been questioned is not strong, only untested, and that he came to belief from the far side of unbelief. Where has avoiding your hardest questions actually weakened your faith rather than protected it?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication. Many protect their faith by refusing to ask the hard thing, and call the avoidance loyalty. The aim is honest recognition that buried doubts do not die, they fester, and that facing them is the path to a tested faith. Go first, naming a real question you have had to face.

objections.objection: Faith is just believing things without evidence, or even against the evidence. That is the whole problem with religion. If you had good reasons, you would call it knowledge, not faith. The very word admits you are believing what cannot be shown.
objections.response: Bell grants that this kind of faith exists and is worth attacking. There is a willful, blind, switch-off-your-brain religiosity that treats doubt as sin and questions as betrayal, and it has done real harm and earned the skeptic's contempt. But that is not what the Bible means by the word, and the skeptic is attacking a definition Scripture never uses. Biblical faith is the same word the New Testament uses for ordinary trust, and it is never belief without grounds. It is trust placed in a person on the basis of what you have come to know about them. You trust a surgeon to cut you open, not with certainty and not blindly, but on warrant, her training, her record, the testimony of others. You trust a spouse, a pilot, a friend the same way, acting on good reasons that nonetheless fall short of proof. All of life runs on exactly this kind of trust. Faith in God is not a different and irrational species of belief. It is trust in a person, grounded in evidence, exercised the way you already exercise trust every day, only aimed at the one the evidence has been pointing to all along.

objections.objection: If I have doubts, real ones, then I do not really have faith, and I should either fake it or stop pretending. A true believer would not lie awake wondering whether any of it is true.
objections.response: This is the most pastorally important objection in the room, and it must be answered with tenderness, because it is the cry of someone who thinks their honesty has locked them out. Hear this clearly. The opposite of faith is not doubt. The opposite of faith is unbelief, the settled and final refusal to trust, the closed door. Doubt is a different thing entirely. Doubt is the wrestling of a person who is still in the relationship, still asking, still showing up to argue with God, which is itself a form of holding on. The Psalms are full of it. The man who brought his sick son to Jesus said the truest prayer in the Bible, I believe, help my unbelief, holding both in the same breath, and Jesus did not send him away to sort out his theology first. He healed the boy. A faith that has never doubted is not necessarily strong. It may simply never have been tested. The faith worth having is not the absence of questions but trust that has walked through the questions and come out still holding on.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the doubt you have never said out loud in church, the question you suspect would get you a worried look instead of a real answer, and what would it mean to finally bring it into the open?
sessions.practice: This week, do the opposite of what shame tells you to do with your doubts. Write down the hardest question you carry about the faith, the one you have been afraid to ask, in plain words, without softening it. Then do not try to answer it yet. Just bring it, out loud, to God, the way the father brought his I believe, help my unbelief. Tell him the doubt directly. Notice whether saying it to him, rather than hiding it from him, changes anything about how it feels to carry.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, we have been taught to hide our doubts from you as if you did not already know them, as if honesty were the one thing you could not bear. Forgive the church for shaming the questioners and forgive us for faking a certainty we did not have. We bring you what the father brought, the believing and the unbelief together, in the same breath, and we ask you to do with it what you did with him, not to reject the mixture but to meet it. Where our faith is real, strengthen it. Where it is doubt, help our unbelief. We are still here, still asking, and we trust that the asking is itself a kind of holding on. Amen.
reflection: Which definition of faith have I been carrying, belief without evidence or warranted trust in a person, and how does the difference change what is being asked of me?
Have I confused doubt with unbelief, treating my honest questions as proof I do not belong, when they may be the very evidence that I am still in the relationship?
What hard question have I been avoiding to protect my faith, and is the avoidance actually making my faith stronger or only leaving it untested?
sessions.teaching: The word faith has been ruined from both directions, and before we can ask anyone to have it, we have to rescue it. From the skeptic's side, faith has come to mean believing things without evidence, or worse, against the evidence, the deliberate switching off of the rational mind in favor of comforting fictions. Mark Twain's schoolboy definition gets quoted approvingly, that faith is believing what you know ain't so, and a great deal of the modern contempt for religion rests on taking that as the actual meaning of the word. And here is the uncomfortable thing the believer has to admit. There is a religion that fits the caricature exactly. There is a blind, willful, anti-intellectual piety that treats every question as an attack, every doubt as a sin to be repented of, every honest objection as the devil whispering, and it has done real and lasting harm, driving thoughtful people out the door and convincing them that to believe they would have to lobotomize themselves first. Grant the skeptic his target. That faith deserves to die. But it is not the faith of the Bible, and the skeptic is swinging at a definition Scripture never gave. The word translated faith in the New Testament is the ordinary Greek word for trust, the same word you would use for trusting a business partner or relying on a friend, and it is never, anywhere, defined as belief without grounds. It is trust placed in a person on the basis of what you have come to know about that person. Think about how trust actually works in the rest of your life, because the faith God asks for is not a stranger to it. You lie down on a table and let a surgeon you met last week cut into your body, and you do it on the basis of evidence, her credentials, her record, the hospital's reputation, the testimony of others she has cut. You board an aircraft and trust your life to a pilot you will never see, on the basis of the safety record of the airline and the existence of an aviation system. You marry a person, promising your whole future to them, on the basis of years of coming to know who they are, and yet without certainty, because no amount of knowing closes the gap entirely. All of life, every relationship that matters, runs on this kind of trust, warranted but not proven, evidence-based but always finally a commitment that outruns the evidence by a step. That is what faith in God is. Not a different and irrational species of belief, reserved for the gullible, but trust in a person, grounded in what the evidence has been pointing to, exercised the same way you exercise trust every single day, only aimed now at the one toward whom the heavens and the documents and the empty tomb have all been pointing. Now turn to the other ruin of the word, the one that lives inside the church and wounds the believer, the assumption that doubt is the opposite of faith and therefore a kind of failure. So many sincere Christians carry their doubts like a secret shame, lying awake wondering whether any of it is true and concluding that the wondering itself proves they do not really believe, that a true Christian would not have these questions, that they are frauds for sitting in the pew with a divided heart. This is a lie, and it needs to be named as one, because it does enormous damage. The opposite of faith is not doubt. The opposite of faith is unbelief, and the two are not the same thing at all. Unbelief is a settled posture, a closed door, the final refusal to trust, the decision to stop dealing with God altogether. Doubt is the opposite of a closed door. Doubt is the wrestling of someone still inside the relationship, still asking the hard questions, still showing up at three in the morning to argue with a God he is not sure is there, and that showing up, that arguing, is itself a form of holding on. Jacob wrestled all night and would not let go and was given a new name for it. The Psalms are full of men shouting their doubts straight up at heaven, how long, O Lord, why have you forsaken me, and those prayers were not edited out for being faithless. They were preserved as Scripture. And the clearest word of all is the father in Mark, who brought his sick and tormented son to Jesus and, when Jesus spoke of believing, cried out the truest prayer in the whole Bible, I believe, help my unbelief. Look hard at what he did. He held faith and doubt together in a single breath, confessing both at once, and Jesus did not stop and say come back when you have sorted out your theology, come back when the doubt is gone and the faith is pure. He healed the boy. He answered the mixed and trembling and imperfect faith of a desperate father, because that is the faith real people actually have. And I have to tell you that I know this from the inside, not as a man who has always believed easily, but as one who came to belief from the far side of unbelief and still feels the pull of the old doubts on certain mornings. I used to think the strongest faith was the one that had never been questioned, and I had it exactly backwards. A faith that has never been tested is not strong. It is simply untested, like a bridge that has never carried a load, and you do not know what it will bear until the weight comes. The faith worth having, the only kind that holds when the diagnosis comes or the grave opens or the dark closes in, is not the faith that never doubted. It is the faith that walked all the way through the doubt, asked the worst question out loud, and came out the other side still holding on, not because the questions all got answered but because somewhere in the wrestling it found that the One it was wrestling had never once let go.

scriptureStudy.note: I believe, help my unbelief. The father confesses faith and doubt in the same breath, and Jesus heals his son anyway, treating honest divided faith as something to be met, not a disqualifier to be cleared first.

Faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen. Note the words assurance and conviction. This is not blind wishing but settled confidence, trust in what is real though not yet visible to the eye.

Jesus invites Thomas to touch the wounds rather than scolding him for needing evidence. He provides the proof and then blesses those who believe without having seen, honoring both the doubter and the trust that follows the witnesses.

How long, O Lord. Will you forget me forever. The psalmist hurls his doubt directly at God, and the prayer is preserved as Scripture, which tells us that bringing the doubt to God is itself an act of faith, not a betrayal of it.
Have mercy on those who doubt. Scripture's own instruction about doubters is mercy, not rebuke, a direct command against the shaming the church so often practices.

Jacob wrestles with God until daybreak and will not let go, and is given a new name. The wrestling is not punished. It is the very thing that marks him, a picture of doubt that refuses to release its grip on God.

Let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the doubter is like a wave driven by the wind. Read carefully, James is not condemning all questioning but warning against double-mindedness, the unstable refusal to commit, which is unbelief rather than honest doubt.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the long Christian tradition of reasoned faith, because the idea that belief and reason are enemies is a recent prejudice that the church's own history flatly contradicts. From the start, Christianity produced thinkers who took doubt and objection with full seriousness. Augustine in the fourth and fifth centuries spoke of faith seeking understanding, a phrase Anselm later made famous, the conviction that one believes in order to understand and understands in order to believe more deeply, the two working together rather than against each other. Thomas Aquinas in the thirteenth century built his entire method on stating the strongest objections to a position before answering them, modeling exactly the intellectual honesty the modern caricature says faith forbids. A serious group should weigh this tradition against the genuine tension that remains. The same tradition also insisted that faith is finally a gift and a trust, not the conclusion of an argument, and held that reason can carry you to the threshold but that crossing it is an act of the whole person, will and heart as well as mind. Read the modern voices who recovered this, C. S. Lewis, who reasoned his way out of atheism and wrote that he was the most reluctant convert in all England, and Timothy Keller, whose work on doubt argued that everyone, believer and skeptic alike, lives by faith commitments that cannot be finally proven, so the honest question is not whether you have faith but which faith stands up best under examination. The discipline of this session is to refuse the false choice between a blind faith that fears questions and a proud reason that thinks it has none of its own. Hold instead that the most honest believer is the one who has doubted hardest and looked longest, and that doubt taken to God, rather than hidden from him, is one of the ordinary ways faith grows from something inherited into something owned.
sessions.caseStudy: A man named Theo had been a believer for thirty years and had never told anyone that for most of them he had quietly wondered whether any of it was real. He served, he tithed, he led, and underneath it all he carried a doubt he was sure would disqualify him if it ever got out, so he hid it and the hiding exhausted him. When the group reached the father in Mark who prayed I believe, help my unbelief, Theo finally said it out loud, and the room did not flinch, and a younger member said quietly that he had assumed Theo was the one person there who never struggled. Theo wept, not from grief but from relief, the relief of thirty years of pretending finally set down. The work for the group is to notice the cost of the hiding, not the doubt itself but the secrecy around it, and what the secrecy had done to a faith that was real all along. Ask your room, what have you never said out loud in church because you were sure it would get you a worried look instead of a welcome, and what has the hiding cost you that the honesty might give back.

memoryVerse.text: Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.

sessions.title: The Call to Follow
sessions.aim: To bring the whole study to the invitation underneath all the evidence and argument, that Christianity is finally not a set of propositions to assent to but a person to follow, and to count honestly both what it costs and what it gives.
sessions.summary: Everything in this study has been clearing the ground, the question of God, the claims of Jesus, the evidence of the tomb, the meaning of faith and doubt. But none of it is the point. The point is a person who, when he met fishermen at their nets, did not hand them a worldview to evaluate. He said two words. Follow me. The first question is why he asks for following rather than merely believing, because you can believe a fact at a distance and never move, and he will not settle for that. Bell takes the strong form of the seeker's hesitation, that this is the catch, that all the reasonable evidence was just the setup for an unreasonable demand, the surrender of your whole life. He grants there is a cost, and refuses to hide it the way the salesmen of cheap grace do. Jesus told people to count the cost, said that following him could divide families and lead to a cross, and never once promised an easy life. But the seeker who fears losing his life to follow has not heard the other half, the strangest promise in all of Scripture, that whoever loses his life for Christ's sake will find it, that the cost is real but the exchange is the best trade a human being can make.
