Then the end of the whole study, which does not resolve into a tidy decision. It comes to rest where it began, with a person standing in front of you, asking the one question the evidence was always leading toward. Not do you find this plausible, but will you follow me.

keyScripture.why: Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men. Jesus does not ask the fishermen to evaluate a doctrine. He calls them to a person and a life, which is what the whole faith finally comes down to, not assent to propositions but the decision to follow.

discussion.q: All five sessions have been about evidence and argument, but Jesus met the fishermen with two words, follow me. Why does it matter that the faith ends in a call to follow and not in a conclusion to accept?
discussion.behind: Open by gathering the whole study. The reasoning was real and necessary, but it was always pointing past itself to a person. The aim is to move the room from evaluating Christianity to reckoning with the One it is about, from a verdict in the head to a decision of the whole life.

discussion.q: You can believe a fact at a distance and never move. Jesus asks for following, not just believing. What is the difference between believing something about Jesus and actually following him?
discussion.behind: Get the room to feel the gap between intellectual assent and discipleship. Many sincerely believe the facts and have never moved an inch. The aim is recognition that the faith is not finished when the mind is convinced, that following is a different and harder and more living thing.

discussion.q: Bell refuses to hide the cost, that Jesus told people to count it, that following could divide families and lead to a cross. Why do you think Jesus was so honest about the cost, rather than selling an easy version?
discussion.behind: Hold the honesty. Jesus consistently made it harder to follow him, not easier, turning crowds away. The aim is to let the room see that a faith that hides the cost is selling something Jesus never sold, and that the honesty about the price is part of what makes the offer trustworthy rather than a sales pitch.

discussion.q: Jesus says whoever loses his life for his sake will find it. How is that not just a religious slogan, and where have you seen, even in small ways, that holding tightly to your life is the way to lose it?
discussion.behind: Land the central paradox. The promise sounds like word play until you test it against experience, where grasping at life, control, approval, security, tends to hollow it out, and giving it away tends to fill it. Help the room find concrete instances, so the exchange Jesus offers stops sounding abstract.

discussion.q: Looking back over all five sessions, where do you actually stand tonight, and what is the real thing, evidence or cost or fear, that stands between you and following?
discussion.behind: Close the whole study with self-implication and invitation, not pressure. Do not force a decision. Invite each person, the leader first, to name honestly where they are and what holds them back, distinguishing an evidence problem from a cost problem, since they are answered differently. End at the feet of the One who calls, not with a tidy resolution.

objections.objection: So this is the catch. All the reasonable evidence and the honest treatment of doubt was just the windup, and now comes the pitch, give up your whole life, your freedom, your decisions, and follow. The reasonableness was bait for an unreasonable surrender.
objections.response: Bell grants the suspicion and refuses to soften the cost, because Jesus never did. Yes, the call is to follow, and following is total, not a hobby added to an otherwise unchanged life, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling a Christianity Jesus would not recognize. He said count the cost before you build, said following him could cost you family and comfort and even your life, and turned away crowds who wanted the benefits without the allegiance. So the suspicion is right that something total is being asked. But look closer at what surrender to Christ actually is, because it is not the loss of freedom into slavery. Every person already serves something, money, approval, appetite, the opinion of others, the relentless project of the self, and these are harder masters than Christ and pay worse. The call to follow is not the exchange of freedom for bondage. It is the exchange of a tyranny you did not choose for a Lord who is gentle and lowly and gave his life for you. The cost is real. So is the freedom on the other side of it, which is not the freedom to do anything but the freedom to finally become who you were made to be.

objections.objection: I am not good enough to follow Jesus. If following costs everything and means being the kind of person he describes, then I am disqualified before I start. I would just fail and prove I was never serious.
objections.response: Hear the relief in this, because it misunderstands the whole gospel in a way that is easy to correct and life-giving to correct. Following Jesus is not first a moral achievement you produce to qualify. It is a response to a grace you receive though you do not qualify. He did not call the fishermen because they were holy. He called them rough and flawed and watched them fail repeatedly, Peter most spectacularly of all, denying him three times, and still made Peter the rock. The whole point of the cross, which this study has been circling, is that he came for people who are not good enough, that there is no other kind of person, and that the entrance requirement is not a clean record but an empty hand. You do not clean yourself up to follow him. You follow him, and the cleaning happens slowly, over a lifetime, by his power and not yours. The call is not to the qualified. It is to the willing, and the willingness need only be the size of a mustard seed and as honest as I believe, help my unbelief.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If Jesus stood in front of you tonight, the real one, not the tame one, and said the two words he said to the fishermen, follow me, what is the one thing in your life you are most afraid he would ask you to leave at the nets?
sessions.practice: This week, before deciding anything, do one honest thing. Take twenty minutes alone and write two lists side by side. On one, write what following Jesus would actually cost you, the specific things, named plainly, no softening. On the other, write what you are currently serving instead, the things you organize your life around now, and what they have actually given you in return. Do not rush to a conclusion. Just let the two lists sit next to each other, and ask which master you would rather have.
sessions.closingPrayer: Jesus, you did not hand the fishermen a worldview to grade. You said follow me, and somehow they left the nets. We have spent these weeks weighing and questioning and counting, which was right, but it was always leading here, to you, standing in front of us, asking. We will not pretend we are not afraid of the cost, because you never asked us to pretend. But we are beginning to see that we are already serving harder masters than you, and that the life we are clutching is slipping through our fingers anyway. Give the ones who are ready the courage to follow, and give the ones who are not the honesty to keep looking. We come to you with the little faith we have, and the doubt that comes with it, and we ask you to make it enough. Amen.
reflection: Have I been treating Christianity as a set of claims to evaluate, and never reckoned with the fact that underneath them is a person saying follow me, to me, by name?

What is the real obstacle between me and following, honestly, an unanswered question about whether it is true, or a clear sense of what it would cost, and how does naming which one change what I do next?
What am I currently serving instead of Christ, and what has it actually given me, and would I rather have that master or the One who gave his life for me?
sessions.teaching: We have spent five sessions clearing the ground, and the clearing was necessary. We asked whether there is a God and found that the world points without coercing. We asked who Jesus thought he was and found a man who left us no room to call him merely a teacher. We asked whether anything happened at the tomb and found a body of evidence the natural theories can only strain to cover. We asked what faith and doubt actually are and found that faith is warranted trust and doubt is not its enemy. All of it was real and worth doing, and none of it was the point. Because Christianity, at the end, is not a worldview you adopt after the arguments come out in its favor. It is a person, and when that person walked along the shore of Galilee and came upon fishermen mending their nets, he did not sit down and offer them a case to evaluate. He did not lay out the cosmological argument or the evidence for the resurrection or a theory of faith. He said two words. Follow me. And the strangest thing in the whole account is the next sentence. Immediately they left their nets and followed him. So the first question this last session forces is why he asks for following at all, why he does not settle for believing, because you can believe a fact and never move. You can be intellectually persuaded that there is a God, that Jesus is who he claimed, that the tomb was empty, and hold all of it at arm's length like a verdict in a case that does not concern you, and change nothing about how you live on Monday. Jesus will not accept that, and the reason is that he is not asking to be agreed with. He is asking to be followed, which is a different and far more total thing, the difference between believing a doctor's diagnosis and actually taking the medicine, between admiring a road and walking down it. Now take the seeker's hesitation at its strongest, because it is honest and it is fair and most people in the room feel it even if they have not said it. The hesitation says, ah, so this is the catch. All of that reasonable evidence, all of that honest treatment of doubt, all of that refusal to shame the questioner, it was the windup, and here comes the pitch. Give up your whole life. Surrender your freedom, your choices, your future, and follow. The reasonableness, the suspicion runs, was just the bait on the hook of an unreasonable demand. And I will not insult you by denying the cost, because Jesus never denied it, and the preachers who hide it are selling something he would not recognize. He told people to count the cost before they followed, the way a man counts the cost before he builds a tower so he does not run out of money halfway up and become a laughingstock. He said following him could divide a family, could cost a man his comfort, his reputation, his very life, that you must be willing to take up a cross, which to his hearers meant the instrument of a brutal public execution, not a piece of jewelry. He repeatedly made it harder to follow him, not easier, watching crowds drift away rather than soften the terms. So the suspicion is correct on one point. Something total is being asked. There is no version of following Jesus that is a mild hobby tacked onto an otherwise unchanged life. But here is where the seeker has heard only half, and the missing half changes everything. The surrender Jesus asks for is not the exchange of a free life for a life of slavery, because the honest truth, if you will look at it, is that you are not free now. Every human being is already following something, already serving some master that organizes the life and demands the sacrifices and sets the terms. For some it is money, for some the approval of other people, for some the appetites of the body, for some the endless exhausting project of building and defending the self. These are real masters, and they are harder than Christ and they pay far worse, and most of them you did not even choose, you simply drifted into their service. So the call to follow Jesus is not the loss of a freedom you currently enjoy. It is the chance to trade a tyranny you never chose for a Lord who is gentle and lowly in heart and who proved what he thinks of you by dying for you before you ever turned to him. And then comes the promise that sounds at first like a riddle and turns out to be the truest thing ever said about being human. Whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. Test it against your own experience, because it is not a slogan, it is a law of the soul as reliable as gravity. The person who clutches his life hardest, who grasps at security and control and approval and will not let go of anything, finds the life going dead in his hands, hollowing out, slipping through the very fingers that grip it. And the person who lets go, who gives the life away, to God, to others, to a calling larger than himself, somehow finds it, fuller and freer than the grasping ever made it. Jesus is not asking you to throw your life away. He is telling you the only way to actually find it, and offering himself as the One worth losing it for. And so this study, like the man it is about, does not resolve into a tidy decision you can check off and file away. It comes to rest exactly where it began, with a person standing in front of you. I came to him myself from the far side of unbelief, and I will not pretend the following has been easy or that the doubts never returned, because both would be lies, and this study has tried not to lie to you. But I will tell you that the trade was the best one I ever made, that I lost a life I was clutching and found one I could not have built, and that the One who asked for everything turned out to be the only master who first gave everything for me. The evidence was always leading here. Not to a conclusion you assent to, but to a question he asks, the same one he asked at the nets, asked now of you, by name. Not do you find this plausible. Will you follow me.

scriptureStudy.note: Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men. Jesus calls to a person and a life, not to a doctrine, and the call comes before any explanation, which tells you the heart of the faith is allegiance, not mere agreement.

Which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost. Jesus tells people to weigh the price before following, the opposite of a salesman hiding the fine print. The honesty about cost is part of the offer.

If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross. Whoever would save his life will lose it. The cost is total and named plainly, but it is joined to the promise that losing the life for Christ is the only way to find it.

Take my yoke upon you, for I am gentle and lowly in heart. The Lord who asks for everything is not a harsh master but a gentle one, which is what makes the total surrender an exchange for freedom rather than slavery.

Many turned back. Jesus asks the twelve if they will go too, and Peter says, to whom shall we go, you have the words of eternal life. Following is not naive. It is the choice of one who has weighed the alternatives and found nowhere better to go.

Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord. Peter's first response is to feel unworthy, and Jesus calls him anyway, proving the call is not to the qualified but to the willing, the cleaning coming after, not before.

Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in. The final posture of Christ is not the breaking down of a door but a knock, an invitation that waits on the answer of the one inside.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the theme of discipleship and the cost of grace, because the call to follow has been cheapened in much of modern Christianity into a single decision divorced from a whole life, and a serious group should see what the tradition actually meant. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, the German pastor executed by the Nazis in 1945 for his resistance, wrote in The Cost of Discipleship the now famous distinction between cheap grace and costly grace. Cheap grace is grace without discipleship, forgiveness preached without repentance, the call to follow reduced to a transaction that asks nothing and changes nothing. Costly grace is the treasure hidden in the field for which a man sells everything, costly because it cost God the life of his Son and costly because it calls a person to follow, and as Bonhoeffer wrote with terrible literalness in his own case, when Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die. Read this against the genuine danger on the other side, the legalism that turns following into a performance of moral effort to earn what was always meant as a gift, and ask how the tradition held grace and cost together without collapsing into either. Weigh as well the long literature of conversion, Augustine's Confessions, the account of a restless and resisting man finally surrendering, and C. S. Lewis describing himself as dragged kicking and struggling into the kingdom, the most reluctant convert in England, because honest following has rarely been a smooth emotional yes and is more often a long, argued, resisted, and finally unavoidable reckoning with a person who will not leave you alone. The discipline of this final session is to refuse both the cheap grace that asks for a decision and nothing more and the legalism that makes following a ladder you climb to qualify, and to hold instead the costly grace of the Gospels, where a Lord who gave everything calls people who can give nothing, and the giving of the life turns out to be the finding of it.
sessions.caseStudy: A young professional named Priya told the group, in the last session, that she believed all of it now, the God, the claims, the tomb, and that she still had not followed, and she wanted to know why she was stuck when the case was closed in her mind. The leader asked a careful question, was the thing holding her back another piece of evidence, or was it a cost. She went quiet and then named it. There was a relationship, and a way of living, and a sense of being in charge of her own life, that she knew following would change, and she had been telling herself she needed more proof when the truth was she already had enough and was afraid of the price. The honesty in the room was its own turning point, because once she could say it was a cost and not a question, the conversation became real. The work for the group is to learn the distinction Priya found, that an evidence problem and a cost problem are answered completely differently, and that we often disguise the second as the first because a question feels more respectable than a fear. Ask your room, where you are stuck, is it really that you are not convinced, or that you are counting a cost you have not admitted out loud.

memoryVerse.text: If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it.

leaderPrimer: You did not have to do this, and the fact that you said yes matters more than you know, especially for a study like this one. So before you open the first session, sit with me for a while, because this study will only go as deep as you are willing to go first, and the most important preparation is not mastering the arguments. It is settling your own heart, and being honest about your own faith and your own doubt. The aim of this series is to take the essentials of the Christian faith seriously, to ask what Christians actually believe and why it is both reasonable and life-giving, and to do it in a way that respects the mind of every person in the room. Notice what the aim is not. It is not to win arguments. It is not to corner the seeker until he has no reply and call that a conversion. It is not to produce a roomful of people who can recite the right answers while nothing in them has actually moved. If anyone leaves this series feeling outmaneuvered rather than invited, the study failed, however correct the content was. Keep that in front of you, because the single greatest danger you face as a leader of this particular study is the temptation to treat people as positions to be defeated rather than persons to be loved toward Christ. Refuse it with everything in you. The most important thing I can tell you, and I want to say it as plainly as I know how, is this. Doubt is not the enemy in this room, and you must never treat it as one. A faith that has never been questioned is not strong, it is merely untested, and the questions people bring, even the hardest and most uncomfortable ones, are not attacks to be repelled. They are the honest reckoning of people who are taking the matter seriously, which is exactly what you want. Say this out loud in your group, more than once. There is no question too hard to ask here. You will not be thought less of for doubting. The person who is wrestling with whether any of it is true is not your problem, that person is the whole point. If you take nothing else from this primer, take that, and guard it for the seeker and the doubter in your room who have been waiting their whole lives for permission to ask the thing out loud. You will not always have a clean answer to every question, and you must not pretend you do. Part of the integrity of this study is the willingness to say I do not know, or that is one of the hard ones, let me think about it and come back, or honestly, the church has not always handled that well. A leader who fakes certainty he does not have will be found out, and the discovery costs you everything, because the seeker concludes the whole thing was a performance. Far better to be a fellow traveler who has found enough to stake his life on but has not stopped asking, than a salesman with an answer for everything and conviction about nothing. When in doubt, err toward honesty and toward humility, and trust that a real question honestly engaged does more good than a slick answer ever could. Now keep the room safe, because depth requires safety, and matters of belief are among the least safe topics there are. People carry things here they have never said aloud, a doubt that has quietly eaten at them for years, a wound the church inflicted that turned them against the whole enterprise, a hunger to believe they are ashamed of, a skepticism they are afraid will get them judged. Any of it can surface, and when it does, the room must meet it with respect and not with a rush to fix or refute. Safety here does not mean everyone agrees. It means a person can say I am not sure I believe any of this without being pounced on, can raise the objection that has stumped them without someone firing a verse at it to make it go away, can admit they want it to be true without being embarrassed for the wanting. Never make a person feel stupid for their question, and never let the group do it either. The moment someone in the room treats a sincere objection as an enemy to be crushed, slow it down gently and turn the room back toward listening. The most persuasive thing your group can offer a seeker is not a flawless argument. It is a community where honest questions are genuinely welcome, because that itself is evidence, of a sort the arguments cannot supply. You will face several kinds of people, and you should know them before they arrive. The first is the genuine seeker, the person who is honestly weighing the faith and has not decided, and this person is the treasure of the whole study. Do not rush them. Do not pressure them toward a decision on your timeline. Give them room to weigh, to come back, to take longer than you would like, and resist the urge to close the sale, because a person argued into the kingdom can be argued right back out, and you want them to come freely or not at all. The second is the new believer, fresh and eager and often anxious, who has said yes but does not yet know what they have said yes to, and for whom this study is the ground underneath a decision already made. Give this person the why beneath the what, and do not be surprised when their new faith has doubts mixed into it, because new faith almost always does. The third is the wounded one, who was burned by a church or a Christian, who associates the faith with hypocrisy or shame or a question that got them shut down, and who is here despite that history, which took courage. Handle this person tenderly, and when the harm they suffered comes up, do not defend the church reflexively. Say plainly, where it is true, that what was done to them was wrong. The fourth is the long-time believer who has never examined what they believe, who can recite it but has never been pressed on why, and for whom this study may be unexpectedly unsettling. Let them be unsettled, gently, because untested faith needs testing, and better it happens here among friends than alone in a hospital waiting room. Now the part that matters most, the part it would be easiest to skip. Your own heart. You cannot lead people somewhere you have not gone. If you walk in as the one who has it all figured out, dispensing certainty to the confused, the believer who has never doubted lecturing the strugglers, you have already failed, because Bell does not stand there and neither can you. He came to faith out of atheism, which means he sat on the far side of this table and meant every objection. He was raised without a father, which means the word Father applied to God has never been easy or sentimental for him, and he will not pretend it is for everyone in your room. He still feels the pull of the old doubts on certain gray mornings. He writes from inside the questions, not above them, and the power of this whole series depends on you doing the same. So before session one, find your own doubt and name it honestly. Maybe you have a question you have buried for years because you were afraid of what it would mean to ask it. Ask it now, in your own preparation, because a leader who has faced his own hardest question can sit beside the doubter without fear, and a leader who has buried his own will either panic when someone raises it or shut it down to protect himself, and the room will feel the fear either way. One more practical word before the charge. Watch the clock and the temperature together. These sessions can go to deep and exposed places, the place where a person admits they are not sure they believe, or admits how badly they want to, and you are not aiming to resolve anyone's faith in a single evening or to corner a person into a profession they are not ready to mean. When something heavy surfaces, do not rush past it and do not let the group swarm it with apologetics. Slow your own voice, thank the person for their honesty, and when it is time, move the room gently toward the practice, the reflection, and the prayer, because none of this finally lands as an argument won. It lands as a person reckoned with. Trust the closing prayer to do work the discussion cannot. End every session there, even when nothing felt settled, because faith does not arrive on a schedule and a room sent out toward the person of Christ is better off than a room sent out with a tidy proof. Resist the urge to tie a bow. The unresolved ending is not a failure. It is the truth about how real people come to believe, slowly, with questions still open, drawn more than driven. Here is your charge. You are not the one who converts anyone in this room, and you could not if you tried, and the pressure to do so is not yours to carry. You are a fellow traveler who happens to be holding the readings, pointing everyone, yourself first, toward the person of Christ, who said follow me. Lead like that. Let the weight of these questions rest on you first and most honestly. Refuse every chance to defeat a person instead of loving them, to fake an answer you do not have, to rush a seeker toward a decision they are not ready to mean. Keep Christ above the argument in your own heart before you ask anyone else to, welcome the hardest questions as gifts rather than threats, and when you yourself doubt this week, say so out loud next session, because your honesty will preach louder than your certainty ever could. The goal is not a room where everyone has decided by the end. The goal is a room full of people, you first, who have asked the real questions out loud, who were not shamed for asking, who saw that the faith is both reasonable and costly and life-giving, and who are standing, freely, in front of the One who is still asking each of them, by name, will you follow me. Go gently. Go honestly. Go first.

faq.q: Is this study going to pressure me to convert before I am ready?
faq.a: No, and it works hard to prevent exactly that. The whole series is built for honest weighing, not for closing a sale, and the leader primer explicitly warns the facilitator against rushing a seeker toward a decision on anyone's timeline, noting that a person argued into the kingdom can be argued right back out. The final session ends not with a forced profession but with a person standing in front of you and a question left genuinely open, will you follow me. You are invited to weigh, to question, to take longer than the group would like, and to come freely or not at all. If you came braced to be cornered, you will find instead a study that treats your freedom to decide, including to decide no for now, as something to be respected.

faq.q: Do I have to already believe to do this study?
faq.a: Not at all. It is written for new believers, for seekers who are honestly circling the faith, and for small groups exploring it together, and it assumes a room with all of those mixed in. The seeker who has decided nothing is, in the words of the leader primer, the treasure of the whole study, not a project to be completed. The new believer who has said yes but does not yet know what they said yes to is given the reasoning underneath the decision. You do not need to arrive with faith. You need only to be willing to ask the real questions and weigh the real answers, which is exactly what the study is designed to make safe.

faq.q: Does Christianity actually have evidence, or is it just blind faith?
faq.a: The study argues, carefully, that it has evidence, and it refuses to hide behind the word faith. The first session treats the existence of God as a real question with real weight on both sides, evidence that points without coercing. The second examines the actual claims of Jesus in the earliest sources. The third puts the resurrection on the table as a historical question, with the empty tomb, the appearances, and the willingness of the witnesses to die as facts the natural explanations strain to cover. And the fourth session shows that biblical faith was never meant to be belief without evidence in the first place, but warranted trust in a person, the same kind of trust you place in a surgeon or a spouse. The study does not claim mathematical proof, which no large question about meaning ever yields, but it does claim the faith is reasonable, the kind of verdict a fair juror reaches on the weight of the evidence.

faq.q: What if I have serious doubts. Can I still be part of this?
faq.a: Not only can you, but the study treats your doubts as welcome rather than as a problem. The fourth session is built entirely around the claim that doubt is not the opposite of faith. The opposite of faith is unbelief, the settled refusal to trust, while doubt is the honest wrestling of a person still in the relationship, still asking. The father in Mark who cried I believe, help my unbelief held faith and doubt in the same breath, and Jesus healed his son rather than rejecting his mixed faith. The leader primer instructs the facilitator to say out loud that there is no question too hard to ask, that no one will be thought less of for doubting. A faith that has never been questioned, the study insists, is not strong, only untested.

faq.q: Is not Jesus just a good moral teacher. Why do I have to think he was God?
faq.a: Because the Jesus of the earliest documents made claims that explode the category of good moral teacher, and the second session takes this on directly. He forgave sins, accepted worship, claimed to predate Abraham, and said what people do with him decides their eternity. As C. S. Lewis argued, a man who says such things is not left to us as merely a wise teacher. Either the claims are true, or he was lying, or he was deluded on a scale that would discredit his judgment about everything, including the ethics you wanted to keep. The study takes seriously the further objection that the claims were added later, and points it toward the question of historical evidence rather than dismissing it. But the comfortable middle option, a humble sage who never claimed anything divine, is not the figure any early source actually preserves.

faq.q: How can anyone believe a dead man came back to life?
faq.a: The third session grants the skeptic's strongest point up front, that dead people do not rise, and that a miracle is by definition the least probable explanation. It does not dodge this. But it then asks the skeptic to do more than prefer a vague natural explanation in the abstract, and instead to name a specific one and watch it strain against the facts. The stolen body has to explain why the authorities never produced the corpse. The hallucination has to explain group appearances. The swoon has to explain a flogged and crucified man convincing people he had conquered death. And every theory has to explain why the eyewitnesses, who were in a position to know if it was a lie, suffered and died rather than recant. The study does not claim proof beyond all doubt. It claims the resurrection is the best explanation of a body of evidence the alternatives can only strain to cover.

faq.q: If the witnesses died for their belief, does that not just prove they were sincere, not right?
faq.a: The study makes exactly that distinction and answers it precisely. It is completely true that sincerity is not truth, and that people throughout history have died bravely for things that were false. But the apostles were not in the position of the ordinary martyr who dies for a report he received from others. They were claiming to be the eyewitnesses themselves, the ones who said we saw him, we touched him, we ate with him. So for them the choice under torture was not die for something you believe but die for something you either saw or fabricated. Many will die for a conviction they hold to be true. Almost no one will be tortured to death to protect a lie they personally invented, when a single recantation would end the pain. That does not prove the resurrection like a theorem, but it removes the easy theory that the disciples simply made it up.

faq.q: What does it actually cost to follow Jesus?
faq.a: The study refuses to hide the cost, because Jesus never did. The fifth session takes seriously the suspicion that all the reasonable evidence was just the windup for an unreasonable demand, the surrender of your whole life, and it grants that something total is being asked. Jesus told people to count the cost, said following him could divide families and lead to a cross, and turned away crowds rather than soften the terms. But the study also presses the other half. Every person already serves some master, money, approval, appetite, the project of the self, and these are harder masters than Christ and pay worse. The call to follow is not the loss of freedom into slavery but the exchange of a tyranny you did not choose for a Lord who is gentle and gave his life for you, with the strange promise that whoever loses his life for his sake will find it.

faq.q: I am not good enough to follow Jesus. Does that disqualify me?
faq.a: The opposite, and correcting this misunderstanding is one of the most freeing things in the study. Following Jesus is not first a moral achievement you produce to qualify. It is a response to a grace you receive though you do not qualify. He called rough and flawed fishermen, not holy ones, and watched them fail repeatedly, Peter most spectacularly, denying him three times, and still made Peter the rock. The whole point of the cross is that he came for people who are not good enough, that there is no other kind of person, and that the entrance requirement is not a clean record but an empty hand. You do not clean yourself up to follow him. You follow, and the change happens slowly, over a lifetime, by his power. The call is not to the qualified but to the willing, and the willingness need only be as honest as I believe, help my unbelief.

faq.q: Why does the study keep implicating the writer instead of just making the case?
faq.a: Because that is the method, and the method is part of the honesty. Bell does not stand outside this as the man who always believed and now explains it to the confused. He came to faith out of atheism, which means he once sat on the far side of the table and meant his objections. He was raised without a father, which shapes how he hears the word Father applied to God and which he will not pretend is easy for everyone. He still feels the pull of the old doubts on certain mornings. He writes from inside the questions, and the study asks every leader to do the same, because a seeker can tell the difference between a salesman with an answer for everything and a fellow traveler who has found enough to stake his life on but has not stopped asking. The second kind is trusted. The first is not.

faq.q: I am a skeptic. Is this just going to be a sales pitch dressed up as openness?
faq.a: It is a fair suspicion, and the study tries to earn the right to your trust by refusing the cheap version of exactly that. It grants the skeptic's strongest points rather than dodging them, that the world does not prove God like a theorem, that some belief really is a wishful crutch, that dead people do not rise, that there is a blind anti-intellectual religion worth attacking. It states the objections at their strongest before answering them, and where it does not have a clean answer it tells the leader to say so. It does not promise that following will be easy or cost-free, and it ends with the decision genuinely open rather than cornered. You are asked to weigh the case as a juror weighs evidence, not to be argued into a corner, and to follow the weight of it wherever it actually leads, including, if that is where you land, away.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I still have doubts of my own?
faq.a: Your doubts are not a disqualification. They may be your single greatest qualification. The study is built to be led by a fellow traveler who has found enough to stake his life on but has not stopped asking, not by someone who has every answer and no questions of his own. Every discussion question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than in a debate to be won, so you are not improvising the case. Your honesty about your own hardest question, named out loud, may be the most persuasive thing in the room, the permission that lets the seeker and the doubter stop hiding. What you do need is to refuse to defeat people instead of loving them, to keep the room safe for the questioner and the wounded and the unsure, to say I do not know when you do not, and to point everyone, yourself first, toward the person of Christ who said follow me. Read the leader primer, face your own hardest question, and trust the material.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for being here, and thank you for the openness it took, because questions of belief are some of the hardest things to talk about honestly in a room. Before we start, three things. First, this is a safe room. You can say I am not sure I believe any of this here. You can raise the hardest objection you have here, and nobody is going to pounce on it or fire a verse at it to make it go away. Second, this study respects your mind. It is not here to corner anyone or to win an argument. It states the hard objections at their strongest, and where the answers are difficult, it says so. There is no question too hard to ask in this room. Third, the writer puts himself inside all of this, and so will I. He came to faith out of atheism, and he still has mornings the doubt comes back, and so do I. We are not standing over the seekers from a safe distance. We are fellow travelers. Tonight we are looking at this together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what the passage says and weighed it as honestly as we can. Now let us bring it home, off the page and into the week we are about to walk into, into the ordinary Tuesday and the three in the morning when the questions come back, because that is where this either matters or it does not.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though it is not all settled, because faith does not arrive on a schedule and pretending otherwise would be a kind of dishonesty. Take what we looked at tonight and sit with it this week rather than burying it. Try the practice. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And if you are still carrying a hard question, good, bring it back next time, out loud, because the asking is part of how this works. Let me pray for us before we go. Thank you for the honesty it took to be in this room.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety and honest doubt, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly. Name plainly that no question is too hard to ask here.
Week 2: Session 1, Is There Anyone There, full discussion and practice on the question of God.
Week 3: Session 2, Who Did Jesus Think He Was, with extended time on the actual claims of Jesus and the trilemma.
Week 4: Session 3, The Tomb, part one, the resurrection as a historical question and the meaning of Paul staking everything on it.
Week 5: Session 3 continued, working through the natural explanations one by one as jurors, plus the witnesses and the practice.
Week 6: Session 4, Faith and the Honest Doubt, recovering faith as warranted trust and distinguishing doubt from unbelief.
Week 7: Session 5, The Call to Follow, counting the cost and the strange promise that losing the life is finding it.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five movements, the scripture index, and where each person actually stands now, with space for anyone moved to take a next step or keep asking.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, the question of God and the claims of Jesus.
Week 2: Session 3, The Tomb, with extended time on weighing the natural explanations as a juror would.
Week 3: Session 4, Faith and the Honest Doubt, faith as trust and doubt as honest wrestling rather than failure.
Week 4: Session 5, The Call to Follow, plus a short integration close in front of the One who says follow me.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, Is There Anyone There.
Week 2: Session 2, Who Did Jesus Think He Was.
Week 4: Session 4, Faith and the Honest Doubt.
Week 5: Session 5, The Call to Follow.

bibliography.title: Mere Christianity
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: The classic case for the reasonableness of the faith, including the liar, lunatic, or Lord argument that anchors session 2. Written by a former atheist for thoughtful skeptics, the pastoral and intellectual spine of the whole study.

bibliography.title: The Reason for God: Belief in an Age of Skepticism
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: States the strongest objections to Christianity before answering them, models the even-handed method this study aims for, and argues that everyone lives by faith commitments that cannot be finally proven. Useful across all five sessions.

bibliography.title: The Resurrection of the Son of God
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: The major scholarly study arguing that neither pagan nor Jewish categories of the time can account for the shape of the early Christian resurrection claim. The historical backbone of session 3. Leader to confirm specific claims before pressing them.

bibliography.title: Jesus and the Eyewitnesses: The Gospels as Eyewitness Testimony
bibliography.author: Richard Bauckham
bibliography.note: Argues that the Gospels rest on named eyewitness testimony rather than late legend, directly relevant to the legend objection in session 2. Leader to confirm specifics before stating them as settled.

bibliography.title: Who Moved the Stone
bibliography.author: Frank Morison
bibliography.note: Began as an attempt to disprove the resurrection and became the opposite, examining the evidence around the empty tomb in a courtroom spirit. A model of the juror posture session 3 asks the group to take.

bibliography.title: The Case for Christ
bibliography.author: Lee Strobel
bibliography.note: A journalist and former skeptic interviews scholars about the historical evidence for Jesus and the resurrection. Accessible support for sessions 2 and 3. Leader to confirm specific claims before attributing them to Bell.

bibliography.title: The Cost of Discipleship
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: The source of the distinction between cheap grace and costly grace and the line that when Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die. The spine of session 5 on the call to follow.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: The account of a restless, resisting man surrendering to God, including the line that the heart is restless until it rests in him. Background for the conversion and the longing that run through sessions 1 and 5.

bibliography.title: Orthodoxy
bibliography.author: G. K. Chesterton
bibliography.note: A witty defense of the Christian faith as the explanation that best fits the strange facts of human experience. A balancing voice on the reasonableness of belief across sessions 1 and 4. Leader to confirm specifics before pressing them as Bell's own.

bibliography.title: Gentle and Lowly: The Heart of Christ for Sinners and Sufferers
bibliography.author: Dane Ortlund
bibliography.note: Draws out the one place Jesus describes his own heart as gentle and lowly, relevant to the picture of the Lord who calls in session 5, the master who first gave everything for those he calls.

bibliography.title: The Case for Faith
bibliography.author: Lee Strobel
bibliography.note: Takes up the hardest objections to Christianity, including suffering and doubt, in interview form. A balancing resource for the honest-doubt emphasis of session 4. Not cited by Bell directly. Leader to confirm before attributing claims.

bibliography.title: Making Sense of God: An Invitation to the Skeptical
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: A prequel of sorts to The Reason for God, arguing that secularism rests on faith commitments of its own, directly supporting session 1's claim that unbelief is not a neutral default. Leader to confirm specifics.

furtherReading: Mere Christianity, C. S. Lewis, for readers who want the foundational case for the reasonableness of the faith from a man who reasoned his way out of atheism.
The Reason for God, Timothy Keller, for those who want the strongest objections stated and answered with the even-handed method this study tries to model, leader to confirm specific claims.
Who Moved the Stone, Frank Morison, for anyone who wants to weigh the evidence around the empty tomb in the courtroom spirit session 3 commends.
The Cost of Discipleship, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, for readers ready to count the cost the fifth session names, the difference between cheap grace and costly grace.
Confessions, Augustine of Hippo, for those who want to sit with the long, resisted, finally unavoidable story of one man's surrender to the God he could not outrun.

glossary.definition: The good news at the center of the faith, that God became man in Jesus, lived the life we could not, died the death we deserved, and rose again, so that whoever turns and trusts him is forgiven and made new. Not advice about how to be good but news about what God has done.

Not belief without evidence but trust placed in a person on the basis of what you have come to know about them, the same kind of warranted trust you place in a surgeon or a spouse, aimed at the God the evidence has been pointing toward.

The honest wrestling of a person still inside the relationship with God, still asking, distinguished sharply in this study from unbelief. Doubt is a form of holding on, not letting go, and Scripture treats it with mercy rather than rebuke.
The settled and final refusal to trust, the closed door, which is the true opposite of faith. Unlike doubt, which keeps asking, unbelief has stopped dealing with God altogether.

The claim that Jesus, after a public execution and burial, was bodily alive again three days later, witnessed by many. The faith stands or falls on it, as Paul himself insists, and the study treats it as a historical question to be weighed.

C. S. Lewis's argument that a man who claimed what Jesus claimed cannot be merely a great moral teacher, but must be either a liar, a lunatic, or the Lord he said he was, which clears away the comfortable middle option.

The doctrine that God not only made the world but actively upholds and governs it, the attentiveness that makes the world a witness to him and makes trusting him something more than wishing into the void.

The unearned favor of God toward people who do not qualify for it, received with an empty hand rather than earned by a clean record. The reason the call to follow is open to the willing and not reserved for the worthy.

Bonhoeffer's name for grace severed from discipleship, forgiveness preached without repentance, the call to follow reduced to a decision that asks nothing and changes nothing, set against the costly grace that calls a person to follow and to die to self.
The whole life of following Jesus, not a single decision filed away but an ongoing allegiance, the difference between believing facts about Christ at a distance and actually walking after him.
The turning of the whole person, mind and will and direction, away from self-rule and toward God, not merely feeling sorry but changing course, the response the gospel calls for alongside faith.

The reasoned defense of the faith, the work of giving honest answers to honest objections. In this study it is always a servant of love and never a weapon, aimed at clearing obstacles so a person can see, not at defeating an opponent.

The core set of historical claims about Jesus's death and its aftermath that most scholars, believing and skeptical alike, accept, used in session 3 to ask not whether the facts are agreed but which explanation of them strains least.

This five-session study, drawn from James Bell's book Believe, walks slowly through the essentials of the Christian faith, whether there is a God and what kind, who Jesus claimed to be, whether he actually rose from the tomb, what faith and doubt really are, and what it costs and gives to follow him. It states the hard objections at their strongest before answering them, it treats doubt as honest rather than shameful, and it never corners anyone. Written by a man who came to faith out of atheism. quoteCards: Unbelief is not the neutral, cost-free default it pretends to be. Everyone is standing somewhere and has to account for the ground under their feet.
You cannot keep Jesus as a humble teacher while throwing out the claims that, if false, would make him no such thing. Liar, lunatic, or Lord.
Dead men do not rise. That is exactly why the empty tomb and the frightened men who would rather die than recant are worth explaining, not dismissing.
Almost no one will be tortured to death to protect a lie they themselves made up, when a single word would end the pain.
The opposite of faith is not doubt. The opposite of faith is unbelief, the closed door. Doubt is the wrestling of someone still holding on.
Faith is not believing what you know is not true. It is trust in a person, grounded in evidence, the same kind you give a surgeon or a spouse.
You are not free now. You already serve some master, and most of them are harder than Christ and pay worse.
